title: Genesis 29:31–35
context: The LORD sees that Leah is hated, opens her womb, and leaves Rachel barren for a time. Leah bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah—naming each from affliction toward praise. The unloved wife becomes mother of priesthood and of the royal, messianic line.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on the LORD seeing Leah hated, and Judah born from praise, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: She appears very ambitious of her husband's love; she reckoned the want of it her affliction, not upbraiding him with it as his fault, nor reproaching him for it; but laying it to heart as her grief, which she had reason to bear, because she was consenting to the fraud by which she became his wife. She called her first-born Reuben, see a son, with this pleasant thought, Now will my husband love me.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 29:32)

reformed.quote: Moses relates that Leah was not ungrateful to God. For a profane stupor so occupies the mind of nearly all men, that, like cattle, they swallow up whatever benefits God, in his kindness, bestows upon them. Further, Leah not only acknowledges God as the author of her fruitfulness; but also assigns as a reason, that her affliction had been looked upon by the Lord, and a son had been given her who should draw the affection of her husband to herself.

verses.text: The LORD saw that Leah was hated, and he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD sees Leah hated and opens her womb; Rachel is barren. Divine sight is compassion for the overlooked, not a contest scoreboard.

Arminians stress that God truly regards affliction and acts. Seeing is not bare knowledge; it is kindness that gives life. Barrenness here is a chapter, not a final verdict on Rachel.
verses.reformedNotes:
“The LORD saw” governs the births. He opens and withholds wombs according to mercy and purpose.

God is not a spectator of the tent’s ranking. He counters Jacob’s “more than Leah” with children, and He remains Lord of the closed womb as well.
verses.keyContrast: Both preach God’s kindness to the unloved. Arminians stress sincere, responsive compassion that regards Leah’s pain; Calvinists emphasize the same mercy as the LORD’s sovereign opening and shutting of the womb.

verses.text: Leah conceived, and bore a son, and she named him Reuben. For she said, “Because the LORD has looked at my affliction; for now my husband will love me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Reuben—“see, a son.” Leah credits the LORD for looking on her affliction, then hopes Jacob will now love her. Faith and ache share a sentence.

She prays her theology aloud. Grace has seen her; she still longs for a husband’s heart. God can answer the first without immediately fixing the second.
verses.reformedNotes:
She names the boy from the LORD’s looking. Affliction is not invisible in heaven.

The hoped-for husband-love may not arrive as she wants. God’s seeing is sure; Jacob’s heart remains a slower story. Reuben is gift, not leverage that binds a man.

verses.text: She conceived again, and bore a son, and said, “Because the LORD has heard that I am hated, he has therefore given me this son also.” She named him Simeon.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD has heard that she is hated and given another son. She keeps talking to God about the same wound.

Classical Arminians honor persevering prayer. Being heard is true; the gift of a second son does not mean she was wrong to name the hatred.
verses.reformedNotes:
Leah names Simeon because the LORD heard her and then gave her a son. The name preaches that God attends the unloved wife’s cry.

“this son also” is surplus mercy. Hatred in the house does not veto the LORD’s giving.

verses.text: She conceived again, and bore a son. She said, “Now this time my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore his name was called Levi.
verses.arminianNotes:
Levi’s name means “attached.” She hopes three sons will bind Jacob to her. The longing for covenant closeness in marriage is not silly; it is still unmet.

Children are not glue. Grace invites Jacob to honor Leah as wife, not only as a mother of sons. The later priesthood will come from this boy, beyond her immediate hope.
verses.reformedNotes:
She interprets the third birth as coming attachment. The name Levi outlives the strategy.

Jacob’s heart still leans Rachel-ward, yet God attaches Levi to Israel’s worship. Providence writes a priestly tribe from a wife still bargaining for love.

verses.text: She conceived again, and bore a son. She said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Therefore she named him Judah. Then she stopped bearing.
verses.arminianNotes:
This time she praises the LORD rather than pricing a husband’s love. The turn is worship: the Giver Himself becomes the sentence.

Classical Arminians linger here with Leah. Grace can move a wounded heart from “now he will love me” to “I will praise the LORD.” From this son comes the royal and messianic line—praise that reaches David and Christ.
verses.reformedNotes:
Praise of the LORD names Judah. Then she ceases bearing for a time. The climax of the four is doxology, not a new scheme.

Reformed gospel already in seed: the tribe of the scepter (Gen 49:8–10) and Matthew’s Christ descend from the unloved wife’s fourth son. God chooses the praised LORD, not Jacob’s favorite, as the royal road.
verses.keyContrast: Both read Judah as Leah’s turn to praise and as the messianic line’s door. Arminians typically stress her grace-enabled shift from husband-hope to worship; Calvinists typically emphasize God’s sovereign choice of this son for kingship and Christ.
